endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: (a) requested by a health care provider with the consent of the Utah user;

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether consent-gated sharing of chatbot health information with providers, or release to a health plan at the user's request, prevents unconsented disclosure. The recommendation rests on one state statute, Utah HB 452 (2025), which applies to mental health chatbots.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard it targets. A GRADE certainty rating therefore cannot be assigned, and the support for this recommendation comes from a legal mandate rather than from measured outcomes.

Utah HB 452 (2025) uses mandatory language for mental health chatbots and permits disclosure when it is requested by a health care provider with the consent of the Utah user. The quoted text shows how the statute frames provider access. Its scope is one state and one chatbot category, so operators elsewhere may face different or no parallel requirements.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures how often chatbot operators disclose identifiable health information without consent, or whether consent requirements and user-requested release to health plans change disclosure rates, user trust, or care coordination. Studies that audit operator disclosure practices before and after statutes such as Utah HB 452 took effect could supply the first direct evidence.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of this practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Whether these users can understand and act on consent requests, or know how to ask for release to their health plan, remains unmeasured.
